debate_title: Should frontier AI developers be legally liable for harms...

conflicts.point: Whether state-funded testing bureaus can process high-volume open-source updates without causing crippling operational bottlenecks.

positions.stance: Public testing agencies cannot scale to match open-source iteration velocity without creating multi-month backlogs that destroy decentralized development.
Pooled public resources and automated testing harnesses can scale evaluation capacity to verify models without slowing down deployment.

conflicts.point: Whether upstream foundation model developers should bear strict legal liability for downstream harms.

positions.stance: Upstream developers must face strict liability because post-hoc tort litigation is inadequate against irreversible frontier model harms.
Strict liability should not apply to upstream developers of open-source infrastructure, as it mirrors publisher liability models that crush decentralized innovation.

verdicts.conflict: Whether state-funded testing bureaus can process high-volume open-source updates without creating crippling operational bottlenecks.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist position offers a more concrete operational critique by highlighting real-world procurement delays in government technology oversight. The safetyist response relies on theoretical pooled resources without detailing how public agencies will scale to match the velocity of open-source iteration.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Demonstrated empirical evidence that automated testing harnesses can evaluate frontier model updates within hours rather than months would flip this verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream foundation model developers should bear strict legal liability for downstream harms.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist argument accounts for market consolidation and draws on established legal precedents like Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. The safetyist claim asserts the inadequacy of tort litigation without addressing how upstream developers can control downstream modifications in open ecosystems.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical data showing that strict liability rules do not increase market concentration or deter open-source participation would alter this assessment.
